name: Central Highland Quichua / Chimborazo Quichua
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

Ross Lesson 1 §2 'Word accent', p.1-3; Lesson 2 note 2 'Final accent in ¿Cancá?', p.2-3.
catalog_quote: Quichua essentially has no suprasegmental* phonemes*: unlike Spanish and English, phonetic* stress or accent is almost entirely predictable, falling in almost all cases on the penultimate (next to last) syllable, and does not need to be written[23]. [fn. 23] There is one very small exception to this rule, in which the accent shifts to the final syllable on the last word in the sentence in some cases, but this does not negate the general fact that accent is not phonemic* in Quichua on individual words like it is in Spanish or English. ... Thus, chaipica is always pronounced [čɑypíkɑ] in CHQ, but seems to be pronounced [čɑ́ypikɑ] in Imbabura, as if it were two words chaipi ca. ... [p.39] Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic*, and always falls on the penultimate syllable. Based on this, we know that words like the following all contain the consonants y and w instead of the vowels i and u. ... batya “trough” bɑ́tʸɑ ... usya “dry season” úsyɑ ... pugyu “spring; well” púɣyu ... causaiyuj “having life” (kawsayyuj) kɑwsɑ́yyux ... p'iñajhuan “with [a] hater” (p'iñajwan) pʰiñɑ́xwɑŋ [Ross Lesson 1 §2] Quichua word accent is very regular, falling as a general rule on the penult (second-last syllable) of each word. In the following examples, the accented syllable of each word is capitalized: aLLIlla CANgui alliLLAchu Ari
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; in Central Highland (Chimborazo) Quichua certain sentence-final focus/topic enclitics (-cá 'and what about', and a related sentence-focus suffix) attract stress to the final syllable of the last word of the sentence.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Sentence-final shift of accent to the final syllable on the last word in some cases (e.g. ¿Cancá? 'and you?', -cá topic suffix usually stressed; another sentence-focus suffix 'normally has the accent on the final syllable in Central Highland Quichua'); (ii) in Imbabura and Upper Napo (not CHQ) phrase-terminator suffixes may be treated as separate words for accent (chaipica = [čɑypíkɑ] in CHQ but [čɑ́ypikɑ] in Imbabura); (iii) in Lowland Quichua consonant loss between the last two vowels leaves accent in its historical (now non-penultimate) position. Ross (Lesson 1 §2) adds that accent may be shifted to the final syllable 'for added emphasis', marked with a written accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (each word penultimate); the exception is explicitly sentence-level (last word of the sentence, sentence-final enclitics). Phonetic transcriptions given are Central Highland Quichua citation forms (bɑ́tʸɑ, úsyɑ, púɣyu, kɑwsɑ́yyux). Corroborated first-hand by Ross 1963/2017 Lesson 1 §2 p.1-3: 'Quichua word accent is very regular, falling as a general rule on the penult (second-last syllable) of each word' (aLLIlla, CANgui, alliLLAchu, Ari), based on Colta, Chimborazo.
new_statements.identity_note: Aschmann's grammar covers all Ecuadorian Quichua varieties comparatively but defines 'Central Highland Quichua (CHQ)' as the Quichua of Chimborazo Province (except the extreme south, which is Cañar Quichua, cana1260), much of Cotopaxi, Bolívar and parts of Tungurahua (excluding Salasaka, sala1272) — i.e. Ethnologue qug / Glottolog chim1302 'Bolivar-North Chimborazo Highland Quichua'; the stress statement is given for Quichua generally with CHQ phonetic forms, and the noted Imbabura (imba1240) and Lowland exceptions explicitly do not apply to CHQ. Ross's lessons are based specifically on Colta, Chimborazo Province speech (1958-59), squarely chim1302.

new_statements.quote: 1.8 El acento. 1.8.1 Graves: El acento en el quichua de Chimborazo cae habitualmente en la penúltima sílaba. Excepciones de esta regla general son: 1.8.2 Esdrújulas: Acentuación en la sílaba antepenúltima: En las palabras que terminan en vocal a las cuales se afija el sufijo independiente de validación -mi suelen acentuarse en la penúltima sílaba. ej. állimi -nirkakuna ''está bien' -dijeron.'; ñukaka shuwanátami munak kani 'Yo quería ser ladrón' [...] 1.8.3 Agudas: 1.8.3.1 Existe un morfema de sujeción /´/ en la última sílaba que connota admiración, sorpresa, entusiasmo de afirmación. ej. ¡Kaypimá ñuka atillpaka kashka! '¡Así que aquí ha estado mi gallina!'; Arí; Unjún; ¿Nachú?
new_statements.translation: 1.8 Accent. 1.8.1 Paroxytones: The accent in Chimborazo Quichua habitually falls on the penultimate syllable. Exceptions to this general rule are: 1.8.2 Proparoxytones: accentuation on the antepenultimate syllable: words ending in a vowel to which the independent validation suffix -mi is attached are usually accented on the [stem's] penultimate syllable, e.g. állimi nirkakuna 'they said: it is fine'; ñukaka shuwanátami munak kani 'I wanted to be a thief' [...] 1.8.3 Oxytones: 1.8.3.1 There is a morpheme /´/ (final-syllable accent) that connotes admiration, surprise, enthusiastic affirmation, e.g. ¡Kaypimá ñuka atillpaka kashka! 'So here is where my hen has been!'; Arí 'Great idea!'; Unjún 'aha!'; ¿Nachú? 'isn't it so?'

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate placement (Aschmann 2020: 'falling in almost all cases on the penultimate syllable') and adds detail the catalog record lacks: the antepenultimate pattern with enclitic -mi on vowel-final words and the expressive final accent (Aschmann's fn.23 mentions a final-accent shift on the sentence-final word 'in some cases'; Naula & Burns describe it as an admirative/emphatic morpheme). No contradiction in placement or type.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent regularly falls on the penultimate syllable. Two stated exceptions: (i) antepenultimate accent when the evidential/validator enclitic -mi is added to a vowel-final word (the accent stays on the host's penult: álli-mi, shuwaná-ta-mi), which the authors attribute to the loss of the pan-Andean allomorph -m; (ii) a final-syllable accent that functions as an expressive morpheme of admiration/surprise/emphatic affirmation (Kaypimá, Arí, Unjún, Nachú). Accent is thus predictable and not lexically contrastive; sec. 1.2.2 adds that /a/ tends to reduce toward schwa-like qualities in unaccented syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress or rhythm beyond the chapter heading 'Ritmo, Acento y Entonación'; sec. 1.9 describes five-level intonation contours (clause-final 2-3-0, phrase-final 2-2, dependent clause 2-3-3, etc.), not word-level secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate accent with validator -mi on vowel-final hosts (állimi, shuwanátami), with a historical note (-mi < allomorph -m after vowels elsewhere in the Andes, accent retained as compensation); final accent as an expressive morpheme /´/ (¡Kaypimá..!, Arí, Unjún, ¿Nachú?). Dialect corpus: Troje Mancheno, Colta and San Juan (sec. 1.7).
new_statements.identity_note: Naula Guacho & Burns describe the Quichua of Chimborazo Province, Ecuador, from oral texts recorded in Troje Mancheno, Colta and San Juan (sec. 1.7 notes minor dialect differences among these); this is Glottolog chim1302 / ISO qug (Chimborazo Highland Quichua), the same variety as the catalog's 'Central Highland Quichua / Chimborazo Quichua' record; Aschmann's grammar covers Ecuadorian Quichua generally with Central Highland tables.

sources.quote: Stress in EcQ falls on the penultimate syllable, and shifts when suffixes are added: warmi 'woman' / warmiman 'to the woman' / warmikuna 'women'. Stress can be used contrastively with the "independent suffixes" /-mi/ and /-ka/ to give emphasis. In this case the "independent suffix" itself is stressed. [...] rinimi 'I am going' / kanka 'and you'
